# Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower and RAM: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=organizations-q009 -->
### Question 1

A company uses AWS Control Tower. The accounts in the Workloads organizational unit (OU) hold Amazon S3 buckets that store audit logs. Developers in these accounts deploy changes with the AWS Management Console and the AWS CLI. The company must prevent all IAM users and roles in the Workloads OU accounts from deleting the audit log buckets. An alert after a deletion is not enough. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on a detective control for the Workloads OU in AWS Control Tower, so that an AWS Config rule reports the deletion of the audit log buckets.
- Turn on a proactive control for the Workloads OU in AWS Control Tower, so that a CloudFormation hook checks the deletion of the audit log buckets.
- Create an SCP that denies the deletion of the audit log buckets, and attach the SCP in AWS Organizations to each account of the Workloads OU.
- Create an SCP that denies the deletion of the audit log buckets, and attach the SCP in AWS Organizations to the Workloads OU that holds these accounts.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an SCP that denies the deletion of the audit log buckets, and attach the SCP in AWS Organizations to the Workloads OU that holds these accounts.

**Deciding phrases.** "must prevent all IAM users and roles", "An alert after a deletion is not enough", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: the company must prevent the deletion, an alert after the deletion is not enough, and developers use the console and the CLI.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict an SCP that denies the deletion, attached to the Workloads OU, because a Deny on an OU applies to the member accounts underneath it.
4. I remove the detective control, because it detects the event when it occurs, and then the bucket is already gone. I remove the proactive control, because it checks CloudFormation stack operations, and the developers use the console and the CLI.
5. Between the SCP on the OU and the SCP on each account, the difference is the work per account; the stem asks for the LEAST operational overhead, so one attachment on the OU wins.
6. Check: the SCP on the OU stops the deletion from the console and the CLI in every account of the OU, and it needs no step per account. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The verb is prevent. An SCP Deny is a preventive control: Control Tower builds its preventive controls with SCPs, [Resource Control Policies (RCPs), and declarative policies](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-control-types-mechanisms). On the OU, one SCP reaches every account of the OU. A detective control reports after the event, and a proactive control checks CloudFormation stack operations.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on a detective control for the Workloads ...": [Detective controls detect specific events when they occur](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-preventive-detective-proactive-defined), so the bucket is already gone when the alert arrives.
- "Turn on a proactive control for the Workloads ...": Proactive controls check resources [by means of CloudFormation stack operations](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-proactive-only-cloudformation), so a deletion from the console or the CLI does not pass through the check.
- "Create an SCP that denies the deletion of ...": It works, but AWS advises attaching [policies to OUs rather than to individual accounts](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-attach-policies-to-ous-not-accounts); here each account, and each new account, needs its own attachment.

**Twin.** If the stem said "must receive an alert when an audit log bucket is deleted" instead: a detective control, because [detective controls detect specific events when they occur](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-preventive-detective-proactive-defined).

**Takeaway.** Prevent points to an SCP Deny on the OU. Detect points to a detective control, which is an AWS Config rule.

**Review.** [A Control Tower landing zone applies preventive and detective controls to registered OUs](2-deep.md#a-control-tower-landing-zone-applies-preventive-and-detective-controls-to-registered-ous-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and has 25 member accounts in several organizational units (OUs). The administrators of each member account have the AdministratorAccess policy and can edit the IAM policies of their account. Last month, one member account left the organization without approval, and the company lost its billing and security controls over that account. The company must ensure that no member account can leave the organization again. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, and attach the SCP to the management account of the organization.
- Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, and attach the SCP to the root of the organization.
- Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, and attach the SCP directly to every member account as each account joins.
- Replace the AdministratorAccess policy in every member account with a customer managed policy that leaves out the organizations:LeaveOrganization action.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, and attach the SCP to the root of the organization.

**Deciding phrases.** "have the AdministratorAccess policy", "ensure that no member account can leave", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Member accounts [can leave your organization or close themselves](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-deny-leave-and-close-recommended), so AWS recommends a Deny SCP on the root of the organization. One SCP on the root reaches every member account, new ones too. Principals in a member account [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps), so the administrators cannot undo the control.

**Why not.**

- "Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, ...": SCPs [affect only member accounts](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account), so an SCP on the management account does not limit the member accounts that could leave.
- "Create an SCP that denies the organizations:LeaveOrganization action, ...": It works, but each new account needs one more attachment, and an SCP on the root is [enforced automatically in the newly added account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-faq-policies-enforced-automatically-on-new-account).
- "Replace the AdministratorAccess policy in every member account ...": The administrators can edit their IAM policies, so they can add the action back. Principals in a member account [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps).

**Twin.** If the stem said "no account in the Sandbox OU can leave" instead: attach the SCP to the Sandbox OU, because a Deny reaches [all the OUs and member accounts underneath it](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-deny-at-any-level-applies-below).

**Takeaway.** To stop every member account from leaving, attach a Deny SCP to the root of the organization.

**Review.** [An action is allowed only if an SCP at every level allows it](2-deep.md#an-action-is-allowed-only-if-an-scp-at-every-level-allows-it-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. To protect its logs, the security team attaches an SCP to the root of the organization. The SCP denies the logs:DeleteLogGroup action. A week later, an engineer signs in to the management account, uses an IAM role that has the AdministratorAccess policy, and deletes an Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group in that account. The call succeeds. What is the reason that the call succeeds?

- The AdministratorAccess policy of the role overrides the Deny statement of the SCP.
- An SCP on the root applies to an account only after it is also attached to that account.
- SCPs do not restrict the users or roles in the management account of the organization.
- SCPs restrict the IAM users in an account but not the IAM roles in that account.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** SCPs do not restrict the users or roles in the management account of the organization.

**Deciding phrases.** "signs in to the management account", "attaches an SCP to the root"

**Why.** The SCP reaches every member account, but SCPs have no effect on [users or roles in the management account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-no-effect-on-management-account). AWS gives this as the reason to store resources in other accounts and [keep them out of the management account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-keep-resources-out-of-management-account).

**Why not.**

- "The AdministratorAccess policy of the role overrides the ...": In a member account the Deny wins even when an administrator [attaches the AdministratorAccess IAM policy](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override), so the policy is not what makes this call succeed.
- "An SCP on the root applies to an ...": A Deny on the root is evaluated for [all the OUs and member accounts underneath it](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-deny-at-any-level-applies-below), without a second attachment to each account.
- "SCPs restrict the IAM users in an account ...": An SCP [restricts permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user), so roles are inside its scope.

**Twin.** If the stem said "an engineer signs in to a member account" instead: the call fails, because the Deny holds even when an administrator [attaches the AdministratorAccess IAM policy](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-admin-policy-cannot-override).

**Takeaway.** An SCP on the root limits the member accounts, not the management account.

**Review.** [SCPs do not limit the management account or principals outside the organization](2-deep.md#scps-do-not-limit-the-management-account-or-principals-outside-the-organization-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs its development, test, and production workloads in one AWS account. An audit finds that developers can change production resources. The company must isolate production from the other environments, keep its audit logs in a separate account, and apply the same security guardrails to every account that it creates in the future. The company does not have a multi-account environment yet. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an AWS Control Tower landing zone, and use Account Factory to create separate accounts for the production and non-production workloads.
- Keep one account, tag every resource with its environment, and use IAM policies with tag conditions and permissions boundaries to separate the teams.
- Create an organization in AWS Organizations, create each account by hand, and deploy a security baseline to every account with AWS CloudFormation StackSets.
- Keep one account, and create a separate VPC for each environment, with no network path between the production VPC and the other VPCs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an AWS Control Tower landing zone, and use Account Factory to create separate accounts for the production and non-production workloads.

**Deciding phrases.** "isolate production from the other environments", "every account that it creates in the future", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Separate accounts isolate production: with separate accounts, [by default, the resources and data](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-separate-accounts-prod-nonprod-by-default) of one environment are separated from the others. The setup of a Control Tower landing zone can create [the log archive account, and the audit account](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-shared-accounts). Account Factory then gives each new account the same controls.

**Why not.**

- "Keep one account, tag every resource with its ...": An account provides [security, access, and billing boundaries](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-account-is-security-access-billing-boundary), and tags in one account keep production and the audit logs inside the same boundary.
- "Create an organization in AWS Organizations, create each ...": It works, but someone creates each account and maintains the baseline, and Account Factory [automates the process of applying controls and policies](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-account-factory-template).
- "Keep one account, and create a separate VPC ...": A VPC separates network paths, not IAM permissions, so developers in the same account can still change production resources through the AWS APIs.

**Twin.** If the stem said "limit who can change production resources in one account, with no other requirement" instead: IAM policies with tag conditions can meet it, because the stem then asks for no separate accounts.

**Takeaway.** Isolation, a separate log account and guardrails for future accounts point to a Control Tower landing zone.

**Review.** [A Control Tower landing zone applies preventive and detective controls to registered OUs](2-deep.md#a-control-tower-landing-zone-applies-preventive-and-detective-controls-to-registered-ous-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company has 12 AWS accounts. Each account receives its own bill, and each team owns one or more of the accounts. The finance team wants one bill for all accounts, volume pricing that is based on the combined usage of all accounts, and a monthly cost report for each team. Every team already tags its resources with a team tag. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Create an organization in AWS Organizations from one account, and invite the other accounts to join the organization.
- Activate the team tag as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the Billing console of each member account.
- Create an organization, create 12 new member accounts in it, and migrate the workloads of each team into the new accounts.
- Activate the team tag as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the Billing console of the management account.
- Attach an SCP to the root of the organization that allows the billing and cost management actions for every team.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an organization in AWS Organizations from one account, and invite the other accounts to join the organization.
- Activate the team tag as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the Billing console of the management account.

**Deciding phrases.** "one bill for all accounts", "a monthly cost report for each team", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Consolidated billing gives one bill: the management account pays, and [AWS combines the usage from all accounts](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-billing-treats-accounts-as-one-for-tiers) to decide the volume pricing tiers. A report per team needs the team tag as a cost allocation tag, and the management account activates it. Inviting the existing accounts keeps their workloads where they are.

- The management account is [responsible for paying all charges](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-management-account-pays-all-charges), and AWS treats the accounts [as if they were one account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-billing-treats-accounts-as-one-for-tiers) for billing.
- [Only the management account in an organization](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-cost-allocation-tags-management-account) has access to the cost allocation tags manager, and the activated tag splits the costs by team.

**Why not.**

- "Activate the team tag as a user-defined cost ...": [Only the management account in an organization](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-cost-allocation-tags-management-account) has access to the cost allocation tags manager, so member accounts cannot activate the tag.
- "Create an organization, create 12 new member accounts ...": It works, but existing accounts can join by invitation, so new accounts and a migration add work and give no extra benefit.
- "Attach an SCP to the root of the ...": [An SCP never grants permissions](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-never-grants-permissions), and the bill and the tag reports do not depend on the permissions of the teams.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each team must keep a separate bill" instead: one organization does not fit, because AWS treats its accounts [as if they were one account](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-billing-treats-accounts-as-one-for-tiers) for billing.

**Takeaway.** One bill and combined pricing come from an organization; team reports come from a tag activated in the management account.

**Review.** [The management account pays one bill that combines the usage of every account](2-deep.md#the-management-account-pays-one-bill-that-combines-the-usage-of-every-account-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company uses AWS Organizations. A network team uses a network account to centrally manage one VPC, including the route tables and the NAT gateways. Application teams in six other accounts of the organization must launch Amazon EC2 instances into subnets of this VPC. Each team must own its instances in its own account. The network team must keep full control of the route tables and the NAT gateways. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Share the subnets of the VPC with the six application accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
- Share the subnets of the VPC with the IAM roles of the application teams through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).
- Create a VPC in each application account, connect each VPC to the central VPC with VPC peering, and manage the routes through a cross-account role.
- Create an IAM role in the network account that the application teams assume to launch their instances into the subnets of the VPC.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Share the subnets of the VPC with the six application accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).

**Deciding phrases.** "launch Amazon EC2 instances into subnets of this VPC", "own its instances in its own account", "keep full control of the route tables", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** AWS RAM shares the subnets of one VPC with other accounts of the organization, and each team launches instances into the shared subnets from its own account. [Participants cannot work with route tables](../facts/ram.md#ram-vpc-participants-no-route-tables-nat), and [participants cannot create, delete, or describe NAT gateways](../facts/ram.md#ram-vpc-participants-no-route-tables-nat), so the network team keeps that control.

**Why not.**

- "Share the subnets of the VPC with the ...": RAM can share subnets with [only AWS accounts in its own organization](../facts/ram.md#ram-share-subnets-only-within-organization), not with IAM roles or IAM users.
- "Create a VPC in each application account, connect ...": It works, but six VPCs, peering connections and a cross-account role are far more to run than one shared VPC.
- "Create an IAM role in the network account ...": Instances launched through a role in the network account belong to the network account, so the teams do not own them in their own accounts.

**Twin.** If the stem said "partner companies outside the organization" instead: subnet sharing does not fit, because RAM shares subnets with [only AWS accounts in its own organization](../facts/ram.md#ram-share-subnets-only-within-organization).

**Takeaway.** Many accounts in one centrally managed VPC: share the subnets with AWS RAM.

**Review.** [AWS RAM shares one resource with other accounts instead of copying it](2-deep.md#aws-ram-shares-one-resource-with-other-accounts-instead-of-copying-it-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. The company stores confidential data in Amazon S3 buckets in many member accounts, and teams create new buckets every week. A security review adds a new rule: principals in the company's accounts must not access S3 buckets that belong to other AWS organizations. The rule must apply to every current and future member account. Which solution will restrict this access with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the bucket belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key.
- Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the principal belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key.
- Set a permissions boundary on every IAM role in every member account that denies Amazon S3 actions on buckets that belong to other organizations.
- Add a statement to the bucket policy of every S3 bucket in every member account that denies access to principals outside the company's organization.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the bucket belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key.

**Deciding phrases.** "principals in the company's accounts", "buckets that belong to other AWS organizations", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The rule limits what the company's own principals can reach. SCPs [control which resources your identities can access](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access), and one SCP on the root covers every current and future member account. RCPs work in the other direction: they [control which identities can access your resources](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access). In the SCP, [aws:ResourceOrgID](../facts/iam.md#iam-condition-key-resourceorgid) is [the organization that owns the requested resource](../facts/iam.md#iam-condition-key-resourceorgid).

**Why not.**

- "Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the ...": RCPs [affect only resources](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-rcp-applies-to-own-resources-even-external-callers) that accounts of the organization manage, so the buckets of other organizations are outside the scope of the RCP.
- "Set a permissions boundary on every IAM role ...": It can work for IAM roles, but each new role in each new account needs the boundary, which is far more work than one SCP.
- "Add a statement to the bucket policy of ...": A bucket policy controls who can reach that bucket, so it does not stop the company's principals from reaching buckets of other organizations.

**Twin.** If the stem said "principals outside the company's organization must not access the company's S3 buckets, even when a bucket policy allows them" instead: the RCP, because RCPs [control which identities can access your resources](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access).

**Takeaway.** Your principals to outside resources: an SCP. Outside principals to your resources: an RCP.

**Review.** [SCPs do not limit the management account or principals outside the organization](2-deep.md#scps-do-not-limit-the-management-account-or-principals-outside-the-organization-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company uses AWS Control Tower to govern its accounts in AWS Organizations. The security team finds that some teams create accounts with the AWS Organizations CreateAccount API in an organizational unit (OU) that is not registered with Control Tower. The controls of the landing zone do not apply to these accounts. The company must make sure that every future account gets the landing zone controls automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Turn on more detective controls in the landing zone, so that the controls also apply to the accounts in the OU that is not registered.
- Use an Amazon EventBridge rule and an AWS Lambda function that copy the control SCPs and AWS Config rules to each account that CreateAccount creates.
- Register the OU with AWS Control Tower, enroll the existing accounts of the OU, and create every new account with Account Factory.
- Deploy AWS Config rules that match the landing zone controls to the OU with AWS CloudFormation StackSets and automatic deployment to new accounts.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Register the OU with AWS Control Tower, enroll the existing accounts of the OU, and create every new account with Account Factory.

**Deciding phrases.** "that is not registered with Control Tower", "every future account gets the landing zone controls automatically", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The OU is not registered, so its accounts stay outside the landing zone controls until you [separately register the OU or enroll the account](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-accounts-outside-not-bound). The fix has two parts. Registration brings the OU and its accounts under the controls, and Account Factory is [a configurable account template](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-account-factory-template) that applies the controls to every new account.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on more detective controls in the landing ...": New OUs or accounts created outside Control Tower stay outside its controls until you [separately register the OU or enroll the account](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-accounts-outside-not-bound), whatever the landing zone turns on.
- "Use an Amazon EventBridge rule and an AWS ...": It can work, but the company then writes and maintains custom code that repeats what registration and Account Factory do.
- "Deploy AWS Config rules that match the landing ...": [Detective controls are implemented using AWS Config rules](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-control-types-mechanisms), so the rules report changes and do not bring the preventive controls of the landing zone.

**Twin.** If the stem said "teams create accounts with CreateAccount in a registered OU" instead: the preventive controls already reach them, but [detective controls apply to enrolled accounts only](../facts/control-tower.md#control-tower-preventive-apply-unenrolled-detective-enrolled-only), so enroll them.

**Takeaway.** Control Tower governs registered OUs and enrolled accounts; create new accounts with Account Factory.

**Review.** [A Control Tower landing zone applies preventive and detective controls to registered OUs](2-deep.md#a-control-tower-landing-zone-applies-preventive-and-detective-controls-to-registered-ous-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. The company stores confidential data in Amazon S3 buckets in many member accounts, and teams create new buckets every week. A security review adds a new rule: principals outside the company's organization must not access the company's S3 buckets, even when a bucket policy allows them. The rule must apply to every current and future member account. Which solution will restrict this access with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the bucket belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:ResourceOrgID condition key.
- Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the principal belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key.
- Set a permissions boundary on every IAM role in every member account that denies Amazon S3 actions on buckets that belong to other organizations.
- Add a statement to the bucket policy of every S3 bucket in every member account that denies access to principals outside the company's organization.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Attach a resource control policy (RCP) to the root that denies Amazon S3 actions unless the principal belongs to the company's organization, based on the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition key.

**Deciding phrases.** "principals outside the company's organization", "even when a bucket policy allows them", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The rule limits who can reach the company's buckets, and the callers come from outside. [SCPs can only impact the effective permissions](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-rcp-affects-external-principals-scp-only-internal) of principals inside the organization. RCPs reach [principals external to your organization](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-rcp-affects-external-principals-scp-only-internal), and one RCP on the root covers the buckets of every current and future member account. In the RCP, [aws:PrincipalOrgID](../facts/iam.md#iam-condition-key-principalorgid) checks the organization of the caller.

**Why not.**

- "Attach a service control policy (SCP) to the ...": SCPs [do not affect users or roles from accounts outside the organization](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-not-outside-principals-or-resource-policies), so a bucket policy can still let them in.
- "Set a permissions boundary on every IAM role ...": A permissions boundary limits the company's own IAM roles, and principals from other organizations do not carry a boundary from the company.
- "Add a statement to the bucket policy of ...": It works, but every new bucket needs the statement, and teams create new buckets every week.

**Twin.** If the stem said "principals in the company's accounts must not access S3 buckets that belong to other AWS organizations" instead: the SCP, because SCPs [control which resources your identities can access](../facts/organizations.md#organizations-scp-controls-which-resources-identities-access).

**Takeaway.** Outside principals reaching the company's buckets: an RCP on the root, not an SCP.

**Review.** [SCPs do not limit the management account or principals outside the organization](2-deep.md#scps-do-not-limit-the-management-account-or-principals-outside-the-organization-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled and adds new member accounts every month. A network team uses a network account to centrally manage Amazon Route 53 Resolver rules that every account must use, including future accounts. An administrator turned on trusted access for AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) in the AWS Organizations console. When the administrator tries to share the rules with the whole organization, the share fails. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

- Share the Resolver rules with the account ID of each member account, and ask each account to accept the invitation that AWS RAM sends.
- Add a resource-based policy to the Resolver rules that lists the account ID of every member account, and update the policy for each new account.
- Enable sharing with AWS Organizations in the AWS RAM console, and then share the Resolver rules with the organization in one resource share.
- Attach an SCP to the root of the organization that allows all AWS RAM actions, and then share the Resolver rules with the organization again.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Enable sharing with AWS Organizations in the AWS RAM console, and then share the Resolver rules with the organization in one resource share.

**Deciding phrases.** "adds new member accounts every month", "turned on trusted access for AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) in the AWS Organizations console", "MOST operationally efficient"

**Why.** The setting was turned on in the wrong place. [You must enable sharing with AWS Organizations](../facts/ram.md#ram-enable-sharing-in-ram-console-not-orgs) by using the AWS RAM console or the AWS CLI, because trusted access from the AWS Organizations console does not create the RAM service-linked role. Inside the organization, [AWS RAM doesn't send invitations to principals](../facts/ram.md#ram-org-sharing-no-invitations), and one share names every current and future account.

**Why not.**

- "Share the Resolver rules with the account ID ...": It works, because Resolver rules [can share with any AWS account](../facts/ram.md#ram-share-resolver-rules-any-account), but each new account needs another share entry and another invitation.
- "Add a resource-based policy to the Resolver rules ...": RAM can share with the organization without the need to [enumerate every one of the AWS account IDs](../facts/ram.md#ram-vs-resource-policy-org-ou-without-ids), so a list of accounts adds work every month.
- "Attach an SCP to the root of the ...": [An SCP never grants permissions](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-never-grants-permissions), and the share fails because sharing with AWS Organizations is not enabled in AWS RAM.

**Twin.** If the stem said "partner companies outside the organization must use the rules" instead: share with each partner account ID, because Resolver rules [can share with any AWS account](../facts/ram.md#ram-share-resolver-rules-any-account).

**Takeaway.** Enable sharing with AWS Organizations in the AWS RAM console, then share once with the organization.

**Review.** [AWS RAM shares one resource with other accounts instead of copying it](2-deep.md#aws-ram-shares-one-resource-with-other-accounts-instead-of-copying-it-4-min)

</details>
